chapterTitle: Balancing SRP and OCP: Synergy and Trade-offs
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute mixed-format lesson. Start with a 5-minute animated explanation of SRP and OCP synergy, using a visual metaphor of building blocks: SRP breaks down a complex structure into simple blocks, and OCP allows new blocks to be added or existing ones swapped without rebuilding the whole structure. screens.title: Balancing SRP and OCP
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore the productive tension between two foundational design rules: the Single Responsibility Principle and the Open/Closed Principle. SRP asks us to give each class a single reason to change, and OCP asks us to add new behavior by extending rather than modifying existing code. Together they reduce the blast radius of change and make systems easier to evolve. You will see a simple, practical path: first simplify responsibilities, then add abstraction points where real variations are expected. We'll use a concrete notification example you can refactor step by step, and we'll show when abstractions help and when they hurt. Importantly, we'll address the frequent trap of over-engineering — creating interfaces and patterns for speculative futures — and name two heuristics to avoid it: YAGNI and the Rule of Three. By the end you'll know how to approach refactoring with tests and how to decide whether to introduce an interface or keep code direct. Consider a real module you maintain now: could breaking responsibilities first make safe extension easier later?

keyIdea.text: SRP makes components cohesive; OCP makes cohesive components safely extensible. Apply SRP first, and add OCP only where real variation or extension is expected.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Balancing SRP and OCP
Balancing SRP and OCP
Design for change by making components focused and then extensible.
In this lesson

You will learn a practical workflow: extract single responsibilities, add abstractions where real variation exists, and avoid creating needless interfaces. We'll follow a NotificationService through three refactoring phases and conclude with heuristics to avoid over-engineering.

Why it matters

Small, focused classes limit the ripple effects of change; safe extension preserves stable code and reduces regression risk.

When to apply

Start with SRP as you encounter complex classes. Add OCP only when you see repeated variation or a clear extension point.

Explore Key Topics
SRP First
Break large classes into cohesive units to lower future change cost.
OCP Next
Introduce interfaces or strategies when you expect multiple implementations.
Avoid Over-engineering
Use YAGNI and Rule of Three as guardrails before generalizing.
Visual metaphor
Building blocks
SRP breaks the structure into small blocks. OCP lets you swap or add blocks without rebuilding the foundation.
Quick note
Refactor with tests. Start simple, then iterate when a real need appears.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how SRP and OCP reduce the cost of change and why they work well together. You will practice recognizing candidates for SRP extraction and be able to name situations that signal OCP is needed, such as multiple implementations of the same behavior. You will also learn to spot over-engineering — unnecessary interfaces and premature abstractions — and apply two practical heuristics to avoid it: YAGNI and the Rule of Three. Finally, you'll adopt an iterative mindset: refactor frequently, drive changes with tests, and evolve abstractions only when they deliver clear value. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic or cue to help you remember when and why to act. Practice with the NotificationService activity will let you move from theory to a three-phase refactor in a codebase, making these ideas immediately actionable.

Checklist

  3. Introduce abstractions only when multiple cases appear.

Tip: Keep each step small. Large, speculative abstractions are the common source of maintenance pain. Use the Rule of Three: wait for genuine repetition before generalizing.

screens.title: SRP and OCP Defined
screens.narratorSegment: The Single Responsibility Principle asks that a class or module have exactly one reason to change, meaning it should encapsulate a single cohesive responsibility. This reduces coupling between unrelated behaviors and makes the unit easier to understand, test, and modify. The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification — you add new behavior by extending existing abstractions rather than changing tested code. The practical relationship is simple: SRP creates small, cohesive units that are easy to find extension points for; OCP provides the mechanism to extend those units without altering their existing behavior. A concrete example: extracting an EmailSender from a monolithic NotificationService localizes email logic. Once extracted, adding a new SMS implementation becomes straightforward by introducing an interface. A common misconception is thinking OCP always requires interfaces from the start. That leads to unnecessary complexity. Instead, favor SRP first; introduce OCP when you see genuine variation. Takeaway: SRP reduces reasons for change; OCP prescribes how to add new reasons safely. When could you apply SRP in your current project? SRP and OCP Defined means srp = one reason to change. ocp = add behavior without modifying stable code. together they make safe, incremental evolution possible.. In practical terms, what each principle demands and how their goals align. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › SRP and OCP Defined
What SRP says

A unit should have a single reason to change. Keep different responsibilities in separate classes so changes don't ripple across unrelated logic.

What OCP says

Design modules so you can add new behavior by extending rather than changing existing, tested code. Use abstractions where multiple implementations are expected.

Misconception
OCP demands interfaces from the start. In practice, interfaces are useful after responsibilities are separated and need multiple implementations.
Takeaway
Apply SRP first. Introduce OCP where repeated or anticipated variation appears.
Concrete example
A NotificationService that both chooses a sender and implements email logic is vulnerable. Extracting EmailSender isolates email code; later, adding SmsSender or PushSender becomes simple because the core notification flow depends on an abstraction rather than concrete logic.
Check your understanding
  • Why does SRP make OCP easier? — Because small units reveal clean extension points.
  • When would you avoid creating an interface? — When only one implementation exists and no clear pattern of variation is present.

screens.title: SRP Extraction Process
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring toward SRP is a sequence of small, test-backed steps. Start by writing or confirming tests that capture the current behavior. That creates a safety net for changes. Next, identify distinct responsibilities — validation, persistence, notification, formatting — and pick one to extract. Extracting means creating a new class with a single, focused A P I and rewriting the original to delegate to it. Run tests and fix any failed cases. Repeat until the original class is a coordinator of focused units rather than a monolith. A concrete example is the OrderProcessor that handled validation, persistence, email, inventory and invoicing. Extracting OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, and InvoiceGenerator makes the processor simpler and easier to reason about. A common mistake is extracting too many classes at once or changing behavior during extraction. Keep each extraction small and covered by tests. The final step is a quick review: are responsibilities single-focused and are dependencies explicit? That review protects against partially-applied SRP that leaves hidden coupling. SRP Extraction Process means tests first, extract one responsibility at a time, run tests, repeat until the original becomes a coordinator.. In practical terms, a practical sequence for extracting responsibilities safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › SRP Extraction Process
Step-by-step
1. Lock behavior with tests
Capture current outputs for key inputs so changes are safe to validate.
2. Identify responsibilities
Look for separate concerns like validation, persistence, and notification.
3. Extract one responsibility
Create a focused class and delegate. Run tests and correct regressions.
4. Iterate until cohesive
Repeat until the original unit only orchestrates collaborators.
Concrete example
OrderProcessor initially does five jobs. Extracting smaller classes isolates each concern. After extraction, OrderProcessor calls small, testable services and only orchestrates their interaction.
Common mistake
Extracting many classes without tests or changing code paths can introduce regressions. Keep changes small and verified.

screens.title: OCP in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Open/Closed Principle is easier to apply effectively when you first consider whether multiple implementations are likely. OCP is best expressed by depending on abstractions — interfaces or abstract classes — and providing extension points such as strategy objects or plugin registries. A practical approach is to delay introducing a formal interface until you see two signs: repeated duplication across classes or a clear requirement for alternative implementations. For example, a Logging class that only ever writes to the console is fine as a concrete class. When file logging, database logging, or cloud logging appear, the third variation signals that introducing an ILogger interface and a registry or strategy is justified. A misconception to avoid is premature generalization: creating an interface for everything 'just in case' creates boilerplate and friction. Instead, think incremental: after SRP extraction, watch for where duplication or change requests concentrate, then add abstractions. The practical takeaway is to prefer composition and concrete classes initially, and introduce OCP measures when there is repeated or forecasted need. OCP in Practice means delay formal abstractions until you observe genuine variation. use ocp to encapsulate that variation while preserving stable code.. In practical terms, when to add interfaces and when to postpone them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Delay formal abstractions until you observe genuine variation. Use OCP to encapsulate that variation while preserving stable code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › OCP in Practice
Practical rule

Favor concrete, composed classes early. Introduce an interface when you see repeated alternative implementations or ongoing change requests that affect the same responsibility.

Signal: duplication
If you find similar code across multiple classes, it's a sign to abstract.
Signal: variation
If the same behavior must work differently for distinct contexts, an abstraction helps.
Example
A Logger that only writes to console stays concrete. When file and cloud logging arrive, create ILogger and multiple implementations, then inject the appropriate one.
Misconception
Interfaces are not free. They add indirection and require additional tests and wiring. Only add them when they simplify real changes.

screens.title: Phase 1 — Apply SRP to NotificationService
screens.narratorSegment: Phase one demonstrates extracting the email sending logic into a dedicated EmailSender class. Begin by writing tests that assert the NotificationService currently sends the expected message for an email type. With tests in place, create EmailSender with a send method that contains the former sendEmail logic. Replace the inline method in NotificationService with a constructor-injected EmailSender and delegate calls to it. Run tests and fix any regressions. This step localizes email behavior so future notification types don't require touching the original service. A common error is moving logic without preserving the same public behavior — that's why tests matter. After extraction, NotificationService is simpler; it decides which sender to call but delegates the actual sending. Consider the benefits: smaller classes, clearer intent, and easier unit testing of sending logic in isolation. The next phase introduces an abstraction so multiple senders can coexist without modifying NotificationService. Phase 1 — Apply SRP to NotificationService means extract responsibilities first and rely on tests to ensure no behavior changes during refactoring.. In practical terms, extract emailsender and preserve behavior with tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Phase 1 — Apply SRP
Before (excerpt)
// NotificationService before extraction
public class NotificationService {
  public void sendNotification(String type, String recipient, String message) {
    if ("email".equalsIgnoreCase(type)) {
      sendEmail(recipient, message);
    } else {
      System.out.println("Unsupported notification type: " + type);
    }
  }

  private void sendEmail(String recipient, String message) {
    System.out.println("Sending email to " + recipient + ": " + message);
    // Email sending logic here
  }
}
After (solution)
// EmailSender extracted
public class EmailSender {
  public void send(String recipient, String message) {
    System.out.println("Sending email to " + recipient + ": " + message);
    // Email sending logic here
  }
}

// NotificationService now delegates
public class NotificationService {
  private final EmailSender emailSender;
  public NotificationService(EmailSender emailSender) {
    this.emailSender = emailSender;
  }
  public void sendNotification(String type, String recipient, String message) {
    if ("email".equalsIgnoreCase(type)) {
      emailSender.send(recipient, message);
    } else {
      System.out.println("Unsupported notification type: " + type);
    }
  }
}
Keep tests around this change and run them after each small extraction to catch behavioral drift early.

screens.title: Phase 2 — Introduce Abstraction (OCP)
screens.narratorSegment: Phase two converts the concrete sender into an abstraction so NotificationService can support multiple senders without modification. First create an interface with a send method — for example, INotificationSender with void send(String recipient, String message). Make EmailSender implement the interface. Then add a Map or registry keyed by type to the NotificationService, where the key is a short string such as 'email' or 'sms' and the value is an INotificationSender. Update sendNotification to lookup the right sender and delegate. Add a new SmsSender implementation and register it in the map. Tests will verify behavior for both email and sms without changing NotificationService logic. This is OCP in action: adding a new sender does not require modifying existing logic, only adding a new implementation and registration. The common pitfall is adding an interface when you only have one implementation. Use the Rule of Three and YAGNI to avoid premature interfaces. After this step you will be able to add Push or other senders with minimal changes. Phase 2 — Introduce Abstraction (OCP) means introduce a small abstraction and a registry so new implementations can be added without touching the existing orchestrator.. In practical terms, create inotificationsender and register multiple senders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Phase 2 — Introduce Abstraction
New interface
public interface INotificationSender {
  void send(String recipient, String message);
}

public class EmailSender implements INotificationSender {
  public void send(String recipient, String message) {
    System.out.println("Sending email to " + recipient + ": " + message);
  }
}
Registry approach
public class NotificationService {
  private Map senders;
  public NotificationService(Map senders) {
    this.senders = senders;
  }
  public void sendNotification(String type, String recipient, String message) {
    var sender = senders.get(type.toLowerCase());
    if (sender != null) sender.send(recipient, message);
    else System.out.println("Unsupported notification type: " + type);
  }
}
Register EmailSender and SmsSender in the map. Tests should cover both keys and the unsupported case.

screens.title: Before vs After: NotificationService
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing the monolithic and refactored designs highlights the benefits. Before refactoring, NotificationService mixed decision logic and concrete sending code: any change to how notifications are sent required touching a single class that might also validate input or persist data. This increased risk and made testing harder. After SRP extraction, sending logic lives in EmailSender. After introducing OCP, NotificationService depends on an abstraction and a registry; adding SmsSender or PushSender requires creating a new class and registering it, but not modifying existing code. A useful concrete contrast: adding a third notification type in the monolith tends to produce more conditional branches and a growing method; in the refactored design you add a new sender class and a registration. A misconception is believing added classes always cost more; while they add files, they reduce cognitive load per class and make each unit easier to test. The real cost is wiring and maintenance if abstractions were premature, so balance is key. Before vs After: NotificationService means monoliths centralize change and risk. srp plus ocp distributes responsibilities and reduces modification surface, at the cost of more explicit wiring.. In practical terms, how srp extraction then ocp extension changes the structure and maintenance cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Over-engineering Risks
screens.narratorSegment: Over-engineering is the practice of adding complexity beyond what is necessary for the current and near-term needs. In code this often looks like interfaces for every class, elaborate patterns for one-off cases, or deep inheritance hierarchies created 'just in case.' These make the codebase harder to read, harder to navigate, and more costly to change. The antidote is two simple heuristics. First, YAGNI — You Ain't Gonna Need It — reminds you not to implement features or abstractions until there's a practical reason. Second, the Rule of Three suggests waiting until a pattern repeats at least three times before generalizing into a reusable abstraction. A concrete example: adding an IEmailSender interface when you only plan to use a single SMTP implementation is usually premature. Instead, extract EmailSender for SRP, then when a second and third sender appear, introduce an interface. Another safeguard is continuous refactoring with tests: if every abstraction is driven by actual requirements and backed by tests, the risk of unnecessary complexity shrinks dramatically. Ask yourself: does this abstraction remove duplication or merely add ceremony? screens.title: YAGNI and the Rule of Three
screens.narratorSegment: Use a short decision flow when you consider creating an abstraction. First ask: is there immediate duplication or a clear need for multiple implementations? If no, follow YAGNI and stay concrete. If yes, document the instances and wait until the pattern stabilizes; the Rule of Three suggests that after a third occurrence the abstraction is justified. Next, decide the minimal abstraction: a small interface or strategy that captures only the varying behavior. Implement it for the current cases and add tests that exercise different implementations. Start by factoring out the shared logic into a helper, test it, and when a third logger emerges, promote that helper into a formal ILogger interface. This staged approach avoids premature complexity while allowing safe growth when needed. screens.title: Logger Example: When to Interface
screens.narratorSegment: A Logger class often illustrates the trade-off. At first, a simple console Logger with a single responsibility is appropriate. It follows SRP: logging behavior is isolated. If a request for file logging appears, adding a conditional may be acceptable. If later a database or cloud logger is requested, now you see repeated variation and duplication. This keeps the codebase simple while remaining open to extension. The misconception to avoid is assuming that interfaces are always better; they are a tool to express variation, not a default design choice. Ask: does this abstraction reduce changes or only add indirection? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore the productive tension between two foundational design rules: the Single Responsibility Principle and the Open/Closed Principle. SRP asks us to give each class a single reason to change, and OCP asks us to add new behavior by extending rather than modifying existing code. Together they reduce the blast radius of change and make systems easier to evolve. You will see a simple, practical path: first simplify responsibilities, then add abstraction points where real variations are expected. We'll use a concrete notification example you can refactor step by step, and we'll show when abstractions help and when they hurt. Importantly, we'll address the frequent trap of over-engineering — creating interfaces and patterns for speculative futures — and name two heuristics to avoid it: YAGNI and the Rule of Three. By the end you'll know how to approach refactoring with tests and how to decide whether to introduce an interface or keep code direct. Consider a real module you maintain now: could breaking responsibilities first make safe extension easier later?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how SRP and OCP reduce the cost of change and why they work well together. You will practice recognizing candidates for SRP extraction and be able to name situations that signal OCP is needed, such as multiple implementations of the same behavior. You will also learn to spot over-engineering — unnecessary interfaces and premature abstractions — and apply two practical heuristics to avoid it: YAGNI and the Rule of Three. Finally, you'll adopt an iterative mindset: refactor frequently, drive changes with tests, and evolve abstractions only when they deliver clear value. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic or cue to help you remember when and why to act. Practice with the NotificationService activity will let you move from theory to a three-phase refactor in a codebase, making these ideas immediately actionable.

This second objectives slide frames what you'll practice during the hands-on activity. You will refactor the NotificationService in three phases: extract the email sender to satisfy SRP, introduce an INotificationSender abstraction and register multiple senders to satisfy OCP, and then reflect on how SRP made the OCP step straightforward. You'll also practice writing or preserving tests before each change so refactoring is safe. We will highlight where over-engineering could creep in and how to apply the Rule of Three and YAGNI to resist it. Finally, you'll form a short checklist: identify responsibilities, write tests, extract, run tests, add abstraction only when variation is concrete. By practicing this sequence you learn not only the patterns, but also the judgment to apply them in real projects. Learning Objectives — Applied means practice safe, iterative refactoring: tests first, srp extraction, then ocp extension when justified.. In practical terms, practical skills you'll practice in the coding activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Single Responsibility Principle asks that a class or module have exactly one reason to change, meaning it should encapsulate a single cohesive responsibility. This reduces coupling between unrelated behaviors and makes the unit easier to understand, test, and modify. The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification — you add new behavior by extending existing abstractions rather than changing tested code. The practical relationship is simple: SRP creates small, cohesive units that are easy to find extension points for; OCP provides the mechanism to extend those units without altering their existing behavior. A concrete example: extracting an EmailSender from a monolithic NotificationService localizes email logic. Once extracted, adding a new SMS implementation becomes straightforward by introducing an interface. A common misconception is thinking OCP always requires interfaces from the start. That leads to unnecessary complexity. Instead, favor SRP first; introduce OCP when you see genuine variation. Takeaway: SRP reduces reasons for change; OCP prescribes how to add new reasons safely. When could you apply SRP in your current project? SRP and OCP Defined means srp = one reason to change. ocp = add behavior without modifying stable code. together they make safe, incremental evolution possible.. In practical terms, what each principle demands and how their goals align. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Refactoring toward SRP is a sequence of small, test-backed steps. Start by writing or confirming tests that capture the current behavior. That creates a safety net for changes. Next, identify distinct responsibilities — validation, persistence, notification, formatting — and pick one to extract. Extracting means creating a new class with a single, focused A P I and rewriting the original to delegate to it. Run tests and fix any failed cases. Repeat until the original class is a coordinator of focused units rather than a monolith. A concrete example is the OrderProcessor that handled validation, persistence, email, inventory and invoicing. Extracting OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, and InvoiceGenerator makes the processor simpler and easier to reason about. A common mistake is extracting too many classes at once or changing behavior during extraction. Keep each extraction small and covered by tests. The final step is a quick review: are responsibilities single-focused and are dependencies explicit? That review protects against partially-applied SRP that leaves hidden coupling. SRP Extraction Process means tests first, extract one responsibility at a time, run tests, repeat until the original becomes a coordinator.. In practical terms, a practical sequence for extracting responsibilities safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Open/Closed Principle is easier to apply effectively when you first consider whether multiple implementations are likely. OCP is best expressed by depending on abstractions — interfaces or abstract classes — and providing extension points such as strategy objects or plugin registries. A practical approach is to delay introducing a formal interface until you see two signs: repeated duplication across classes or a clear requirement for alternative implementations. For example, a Logging class that only ever writes to the console is fine as a concrete class. When file logging, database logging, or cloud logging appear, the third variation signals that introducing an ILogger interface and a registry or strategy is justified. A misconception to avoid is premature generalization: creating an interface for everything 'just in case' creates boilerplate and friction. Instead, think incremental: after SRP extraction, watch for where duplication or change requests concentrate, then add abstractions. The practical takeaway is to prefer composition and concrete classes initially, and introduce OCP measures when there is repeated or forecasted need. OCP in Practice means delay formal abstractions until you observe genuine variation. use ocp to encapsulate that variation while preserving stable code.. In practical terms, when to add interfaces and when to postpone them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Phase one demonstrates extracting the email sending logic into a dedicated EmailSender class. Begin by writing tests that assert the NotificationService currently sends the expected message for an email type. With tests in place, create EmailSender with a send method that contains the former sendEmail logic. Replace the inline method in NotificationService with a constructor-injected EmailSender and delegate calls to it. Run tests and fix any regressions. This step localizes email behavior so future notification types don't require touching the original service. A common error is moving logic without preserving the same public behavior — that's why tests matter. After extraction, NotificationService is simpler; it decides which sender to call but delegates the actual sending. Consider the benefits: smaller classes, clearer intent, and easier unit testing of sending logic in isolation. The next phase introduces an abstraction so multiple senders can coexist without modifying NotificationService. In practical terms, extract emailsender and preserve behavior with tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Over-engineering is the practice of adding complexity beyond what is necessary for the current and near-term needs. In code this often looks like interfaces for every class, elaborate patterns for one-off cases, or deep inheritance hierarchies created 'just in case.' These make the codebase harder to read, harder to navigate, and more costly to change. The antidote is two simple heuristics. First, YAGNI — You Ain't Gonna Need It — reminds you not to implement features or abstractions until there's a practical reason. Second, the Rule of Three suggests waiting until a pattern repeats at least three times before generalizing into a reusable abstraction. A concrete example: adding an IEmailSender interface when you only plan to use a single SMTP implementation is usually premature. Instead, extract EmailSender for SRP, then when a second and third sender appear, introduce an interface. Another safeguard is continuous refactoring with tests: if every abstraction is driven by actual requirements and backed by tests, the risk of unnecessary complexity shrinks dramatically. Ask yourself: does this abstraction remove duplication or merely add ceremony?
